series.title: Python Warts and All
series.description: A mini-book series exploring what's great and what's frustrating about Python. Not inflammatory, well ... maybe a little. The goal is constructive discussion.
series.tone: Opinionated but fair. Direct. Draw on real experience — not just docs. Use concrete examples. Each post has a 'good' section and a 'warts' section. Aim for 600-900 words. Write in first person.

good: dict, list, tuple, set literals are concise and readable
JSON compatibility means Python data structures translate directly
Compare to Java: nested HashMap requires type declarations on both sides
Universal appeal — like pop music, everyone understands Python literals even across languages
The REPL shows you the structure immediately
warts: Tuple trailing comma surprise: (1) is an int, (1,) is a tuple — this trips up everyone
Empty set syntax: {} creates a dict, NOT a set. You must write set()
No frozendict in stdlib — you have to use third-party or tuple-of-tuples for hashable dicts
The word 'dictionary' — every other language calls it a map or hash. Python insists on dictionary.
Limited immutable data structures out of the box — no persistent data structures like Clojure

links.text: Java nested HashMap example (what we're avoiding)

good: Dunder (double underscore) methods let you plug into Python's built-in syntax
len(obj) calls obj.__len__() — this means any object can behave like a built-in
Operator overloading feels natural: __add__, __eq__, __lt__
__repr__ and __str__ — two levels of string representation for different contexts
Everything is an object, including functions and classes
Context managers via __enter__ / __exit__ are elegant
warts: Magic method proliferation — there are over 80 dunder methods. Nobody memorizes them all.
__new__ vs __init__ confusion — __new__ creates the object, __init__ initializes it. Most people never need __new__ but it exists to bite you.
__slots__ can optimize memory but breaks some Python conventions and surprises people
Comparison methods: if you define __eq__ you should probably define __hash__ too, or your object becomes unhashable silently
deepcopy complexity — __copy__ vs __deepcopy__ is non-obvious
Descriptors (__get__, __set__, __delete__) are powerful but almost nobody understands them correctly

good: List comprehensions: [x*2 for x in items if x > 0] — readable and Pythonic
Dict comprehensions: {k: v for k, v in pairs}
Set comprehensions: {x.lower() for x in words}
Generator expressions: (x*2 for x in items) — lazy, memory-efficient
Faster than equivalent for loops in CPython due to bytecode optimization
Filter + transform in one expression is expressive and functional
warts: Nested comprehensions are a readability disaster: [[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(4)]
The walrus operator := in comprehensions is clever but hard to read: [y := f(x), y**2, y**3]
No easy way to get 'the first matching item' — you write next(x for x in items if pred(x)) and it raises StopIteration if empty
No comprehension syntax for flattening: you need itertools.chain or nested comprehensions
Generator expressions are stateful and single-use — passing one to two functions is a bug waiting to happen
Leaking variables: in Python 2, list comprehensions leaked their loop variable. Fixed in Python 3, but the muscle memory persists.

good: yield turns any function into a lazy iterator — memory-efficient pipeline
yield from delegates to a sub-generator, enabling composable generators
Processing infinite or huge streams without loading everything into memory
Generator expressions as arguments: sum(x*x for x in range(1000000))
send() and throw() make generators a lightweight coroutine mechanism
Readable data pipeline: read -> parse -> filter -> transform, all lazy
warts: Can only iterate once — this surprises everyone. list(gen); list(gen) gives [] on the second call.
Hard to debug — you can't print a generator, you have to consume it
No peek without consuming: you need itertools.islice(gen, 1) or next() with a default
Generator vs iterator confusion — a generator is an iterator, but not all iterators are generators
send() and throw() are obscure and mostly replaced by async/await now
StopIteration propagation inside a generator silently terminates it in Python 3.7+ (PEP 479)
The three types of 'generators' — generator functions, generator expressions, and generator objects — add terminology overhead

good: The standard REPL is always available — no setup needed
_ holds the last result — useful for quick calculations
dir() and help() turn the REPL into interactive documentation
IPython/Jupyter: tab completion, magic commands, inline plots, %timeit, %pdb
Python's introspective nature makes REPL exploration natural
Quick prototyping — test an idea in 30 seconds without a file
warts: Multi-line editing in the standard REPL is painful — indentation errors are unrecoverable without retyping
No persistent history across sessions in the standard REPL (IPython saves history, stdlib doesn't by default)
Pasting multi-line code often fails due to indentation requirements
No easy way to save a REPL session to a file (IPython %save helps but isn't universal)
Standard REPL has no syntax highlighting, no auto-complete — you need IPython for a modern experience
The gap between standard REPL and IPython/Jupyter is huge — beginners get the bad experience

good: Gradual typing — add types incrementally, no big bang migration
Modern syntax (3.10+): int | None instead of Optional[int]; list[int] instead of List[int]
Protocol for structural subtyping — duck typing with documentation
TypeVar and Generic for reusable typed containers
TypedDict for typed dictionaries without full class overhead
dataclasses with type hints are clean and boilerplate-free
mypy, pyright, and pytype all provide static analysis
warts: Types are not enforced at runtime — def f(x: int): pass; f('oops') works fine
Optional[X] vs X | None — two syntaxes for the same thing, era-dependent
Complex types become unreadable: Callable[[int, str], Optional[Dict[str, List[Tuple[int, ...]]]]]
TypedDict vs dataclass vs NamedTuple vs attrs vs pydantic — too many options for structured data
The typing module itself is a wart — List, Dict, Tuple are deprecated but still everywhere
runtime_checkable Protocol only checks method names, not signatures — false safety
Type narrowing edge cases: mypy and pyright disagree on some valid patterns
No built-in way to enforce types at runtime without a library (pydantic fills this gap)

good: async/await syntax is clear and readable compared to callback soup
asyncio enables high-concurrency I/O without threads
FastAPI, aiohttp, and httpx make async web development excellent
asyncio.gather() for concurrent tasks is elegant
async context managers and async iterators are well-designed
Task groups (Python 3.11+) improve structured concurrency
warts: Async is viral — one async call forces everything up the stack to be async
Blocking I/O in an async context silently degrades performance — no warning by default
Three concurrency models (threading, multiprocessing, asyncio) with different use cases and non-trivial tradeoffs
The GIL means threads don't actually parallelize CPU work — async doesn't help with CPU-bound tasks either
asyncio.run() vs event loops vs get_event_loop() — the API evolved publicly and shows its seams
Mixing sync and async code requires run_in_executor() which is cumbersome
async generators are subtly different from regular generators in teardown behavior
Debugging async code is harder — stack traces are less informative

good: PyPI has over 500,000 packages — the ecosystem is enormous
uv (2024) is a revelation: blazing fast, replaces pip/venv/pyenv in one tool
pyproject.toml is a clean, standard project configuration format
Virtual environments are a solved problem — venv is built in
Wheels make binary distribution practical
pip install is so simple it democratized software distribution
warts: The tooling history is a graveyard: setup.py → setup.cfg → pyproject.toml, distutils → setuptools → flit → poetry → hatch → rye → uv
pip's dependency resolver was broken for years — it would happily install conflicting versions
pip install in a system Python can break your OS on some Linux distros (now blocked with PEP 668)
Too many competing tools with overlapping purposes: conda, poetry, pipenv, pyenv, virtualenv, venv
Publishing to PyPI requires understanding twine, build backends, and trusted publishing
No standard way to lock dependencies until pip-tools/poetry/uv popularized lock files
PYTHONPATH manipulation is a footgun that persists in many projects

links.text: uv — the new Python package manager

good: Python's backwards compatibility commitment within major versions is strong
The deprecation cycle (usually 2 releases) gives migration time
pyupgrade automates syntax modernization
The community produces excellent tooling: black, ruff, mypy all handle maintenance tasks
Python 3.12+ has significantly improved error messages
SECURITY fixes are backported to maintained versions
warts: The Python 2 → 3 migration was a decade-long disaster that fractured the ecosystem
__future__ imports as a migration band-aid: from __future__ import annotations
Minor version breaking changes: walrus operator in 3.8, structural pattern matching in 3.10 — production code must track Python versions carefully
Deprecation warnings are often invisible in production — warnings are silenced by default
C extension maintenance is painful — binary compatibility breaks across Python minor versions
No built-in upgrade path: pip install --upgrade doesn't update the Python version itself
pyenv, asdf, and mise all solve Python version management differently — no canonical answer

good: Python is the lingua franca of scripting — available everywhere
Typer (built on Click) makes building typed CLIs effortless
Rich makes terminal output beautiful with one import
click + rich is a killer combo for production CLIs
Shebang support: #!/usr/bin/env python3
sys.argv is simple; argparse works for basic cases
uv run script.py can run a script with inline dependencies (PEP 723)
warts: Distributing standalone scripts is painful — users need Python installed, the right version, and the right packages
argparse is extremely verbose for simple CLIs — it requires writing 3 lines per argument
The if __name__ == '__main__': pattern is an awkward entry point convention
sys.path manipulation is a common script anti-pattern that causes hard-to-debug import errors
Click's decorator-heavy style makes functions hard to test in isolation
PyInstaller/Nuitka produce large binaries and have complex edge cases
No standard way to write cross-platform scripts — Windows vs Unix path handling is manual
